Vignette: Nari, Age 57

Nari has delivered thousands of babies over the course of her career. She knows the weight of a newborn in her hands, the particular silence before a first cry, the way a mother's face changes the moment she understands that everything is going to be all right. For more than thirty years, she has been the steady presence in the room - the one who knows what to do. It is harder, now, to recognize herself in that description.

Two years ago, Nari was attacked and raped by a colleague after a late shift at the hospital where she has worked for most of her adult life. The man was someone she had known for years, someone she had eaten lunch with, someone whose children she had asked about in the corridor. She had stayed late to finish paperwork. The building was mostly empty. She has gone over those particular facts many hundreds of times since, rearranging them as though a different sequence might produce a different ending.

She did not tell her husband for six weeks. She told no one. She showered every morning with a thoroughness that felt more like punishment than hygiene, and she went to work, and she caught babies, and she drove home, and she sat at the dinner table and answered questions about her day. She describes this period now with a kind of bewildered disbelief - not at what happened to her, but at her own capacity to continue functioning while something inside her had gone completely silent.

When she finally did tell her husband, his response was loving and careful, and she found she could not tolerate it. His gentleness felt like confirmation of how broken she had become. She began sleeping in the spare room, telling him she was restless, that she didn't want to disturb him. The physical distance has remained. She cannot bear to be touched, even briefly, even a hand on her shoulder, without her body flooding with a panic that she describes as having no ceiling - it simply rises and does not stop.

At work, Nari functions, but the functioning costs her enormously. She has requested a schedule that minimizes her contact with male colleagues, offering administrative reasons she has carefully prepared. She avoids the corridor near the staff room where the assault occurred, adding several minutes to every journey through the ward. When she is with a labouring woman and something shifts unexpectedly - a sudden cry, a loss of control, a body that is no longer cooperating - she sometimes feels herself leave the room in some essential way, watching from a distance while her hands continue their practiced work. She comes back. She always comes back. But the dissociation frightens her deeply, because in her profession, absence is not something she can afford.

She sleeps poorly and wakes most nights between two and four in the morning with her heart already racing, the details of the assault arranged in her mind with a vividness that feels less like memory and more like repetition - as though it is simply happening again, in the dark, in her own bedroom. She lies still and waits for it to pass. She has become skilled at waiting.

Nari grew up in a culture and a family where endurance was understood as a form of dignity, and she carries that understanding with a genuine conviction that is also, at times, a prison. She has not reported the assault. She has not spoken to anyone at the hospital. She presents for therapy now because her daughter, who lives abroad and noticed something altered in her mother's voice over months of phone calls, asked her directly whether she was all right. Nari told her the truth. It was, she says quietly, the first time she had said it out loud to someone who loved her, and the relief of it - and the grief of it - were so enormous and so tangled together that she could not tell them apart.

She sits in the therapy room with her hands folded in her lap and the careful posture of a woman who has spent a lifetime being competent, and she looks, for the first time in two years, like someone who is willing to be found.
